Verbs With Infinitives in Negative and Interrogative Forms: Have to and Need to
You can use a verb after an infinitive to express a purpose.

Infinitive verbs have two characteristics:
  • The word to goes before the base form of the verb.
  • We do not conjugate infinitive verbs. This mean that we do not add –s, -es, -ed or -ing at the end.
Take a look at the following sentences and pay attention to the infinitive verbs to find, to display and to send.

Examples:
He doesn't have to send the information.
I need to find this information now.
Do you need to read this book?

We can use infinitive verbs after other verbs to indicate a purpose or something that has to be done. There are many verbs that are followed by infinitives and two of the most common ones are the verbs ‘have' and ‘need'. We use these verbs to indicate obligation or strong advice.
This is the structure you use in affirmative sentences:

Examples:
We have to look for more information about basic types.
I need to read this article about dynamic and static typing.

Gerunds After Certain Verbs: Admit, Avoid, Continue
Some verbs are followed by a gerund which is the ing form of a verb.

When we use two verbs in the same sentence, sometimes, the second verb takes its ing form. There are some specific verbs that are followed by gerunds. The most common verbs followed by a gerund are these: avoid, continue, admit, enjoy, consider, miss, imagine, suggest and like.

Word Formation of Nouns: Suffixes -tion and - ity
A suffix is a group of letters located at the end of a word. A suffix can make a new word in one of two ways:

• Inflectional (grammatical): for example, changing singular to plural (dog → dogs), or changing present tense to past tense (walk → walked).
  • Derivational (the new word has a new meaning, "derived" from the original word): for example, teach → teacher

Noun suffixes: tion
When you add a suffix to a verb form you can create a noun.

Examples:
Transport- transportation
Create- creation
Invent- invention
Inform-information

Noun suffixes: ity
When you add a suffix to an adjective you can create a noun.

Marianne: Hey Robert! I have an exam tomorrow for the declarative computation model class, and I need to understand basic types and dynamic and static typing. Do you have to go somewhere now or can you help me?
Robert: I can help you. You don't have to panic, these topics are easy. First of all, you need to know that a basic data type is a basic building block that we use in programming languages. I suggest reading the programming book to get to know all the basic data types.

Marianne: Yes! I'm reading it now, but there's a lot of information and I don't understand everything thoroughly.
Robert: Do you need me to help you go over the basic types?
Marianne: Let me tell you what I know first. The first type is numbers. They can be integer of floating numbers. Then, we have Booleans that can be either true or false. I know there's also records that are compound data structures. This means that records are a label followed by a group of features like atoms, integers or Booleans. That's all I remember, sorry.
Robert: You don't have to worry. I can continue explaining. You also need to learn about strings which are lists of character codes. You can write them in double quotes. We also have procedures that are the values of the procedure type. For this type, we declare a new procedure and then bind it to an identifier. I admit not knowing all of the basic data types, but I think these are the ones you need to keep in mind.

Marianne: Thank you! I'm taking notes of everything. Now, I want to avoid having the wrong idea about dynamic and static typing. Do I need to understand these types thoroughly before I start programming? I know this is your specialty.
Robert: Not necessarily. Dynamic and static typing only refer to the way a programming language works. Static typed programming languages do not need to define their variables before being used. You only have to declare a variable before you employ it. On the other hand, in dynamic typed programming languages we have to define variables before we use them. That's all.
Marianne: Thank you so much for your help!
